item.title: Tearing Down a SQL Slammer-Style Worm: 376 Bytes of UDP
item.description:
The companion to my wg2 RAT teardown is a 2003-era worm: an SQL Slammer / Sapphire style sample. For my reverse engineering course I produced a fully commented disassembly plus a stack-layout diagram, and this post is the condensed version.

It's a nice contrast with wg2. wg2 is a big C++ program with a command loop. Slammer is 376 bytes with no C2, no persistence and no commands. It does one thing, forever.

What it does, in one breath

A single UDP packet to SQL Server's resolution service (UDP 1434) overflows a stack buffer, redirects the return address to a JMP ESP gadget in sqlsort.dll, and lands in the worm body. The worm then resolves the few APIs it needs, opens a UDP socket, and sprays copies of itself at pseudo-random IPv4 addresses until the machine is turned off.

overflow 1434/udp -> RET to JMP ESP -> shellcode on stack
  -> build API names on the stack -> LoadLibraryA / GetProcAddress
  -> GetTickCount (seed) -> socket(UDP) -> sendto() in an endless loop

I'm describing behavior and structure for defenders and students. I left out the full packet bytes on purpose.

Getting control

The first byte of the packet selects the vulnerable code path in the SQL Server parser. A long run of 0x01 filler overruns the buffer, and the saved return address is replaced with 0x42B0C9DC, a JMP ESP inside sqlsort.dll. When the function returns, execution lands on ESP, which points at the worm. A short jmp hops over embedded data into a NOP sled.

The worm doesn't get "called". It's reached by corrupting a return, which is why the stack matters so much for this sample.

The stack is the data section

There's no data segment and no import table. First the worm carves out workspace by pushing 0x01010101 24 times (96 bytes) and sets EBP = ESP. Everything after that is an EBP-relative local variable. The filler value is chosen so the payload has no null bytes, which would truncate the overflow, and the worm even builds 0x04000000 with an XOR instead of writing the zeros.

mov  eax, 01010101h
xor  ecx, ecx
mov  cl, 18h          ; 24 iterations
L: push eax
   loop L             ; 96 bytes of workspace
xor  eax, 05010101h   ; -> 04000000h with no null bytes in the code
push eax
mov  ebp, esp

Stack layout

EBP-0x54  UDP socket handle
EBP-0x50  sockaddr_in (random IP + port 1434)
EBP-0x4C  PRNG seed / state  (starts from GetTickCount)
EBP-0x48..0x40  saved handles: kernel32, GetTickCount name ptr, ws2_32
EBP-0x3C  "sendto"
EBP-0x34  "socket"
EBP-0x2C  "kernel32.dll"
EBP-0x20  "GetTickCount"
EBP-0x10  "ws2_32.dll"

Strings built backwards

API names are pushed as little-endian dwords, last chunk first, so they read correctly in memory. Short endings use a 16-bit mov cx so the upper bytes stay zero and the string is null-terminated for free.

push ecx              ; NUL
push 6C6C642Eh        ; ".dll"
push 32336C65h        ; "el32"
push 6E72656Bh        ; "kern"  -> kernel32.dll

That's the main tell when you're analyzing it: a long run of push imm32 with printable ASCII constants means stack strings, and tools like strings will never see them.

Finding its APIs

With no imports, the worm borrows sqlsort.dll's own import table. It calls LoadLibraryA through a known IAT slot for kernel32.dll and ws2_32.dll, then calls GetProcAddress through another slot. Because that slot differs between builds, it checks that the target starts with the expected prologue bytes (55 8B EC 51) and falls back to a second address if not.

esi = [IAT: LoadLibraryA]     ; call [esi]
esi = [IAT: GetProcAddress?]  ; check first dword == 51EC8B55h
                              ; no match -> use the backup slot

It resolves GetTickCount and calls it. The return value isn't for timing, it's the seed for the target generator. Then it resolves socket, creates a UDP socket (AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, protocol 17) and resolves sendto, keeping the function pointer in ESI for the rest of its life.

Picking victims without a multiply

The target generator is a linear congruential generator, seed = seed * 214013 + increment. Instead of imul, the worm builds the multiplier from lea, shifts, an add and a sub, which keeps the encoding tiny and free of null bytes:

lea  ecx, [eax+eax*2]   ; 3x
lea  edx, [eax+ecx*4]   ; 13x
shl  edx, 4             ; 208x
add  edx, eax           ; 209x
shl  edx, 8             ; 53504x
sub  edx, eax           ; 53503x
lea  eax, [eax+edx*4]   ; 214013x   (0x343FD)
add  eax, ebx           ; + increment
mov  [ebp-4Ch], eax     ; new state, also the next target IP

I like this part because the whole generator is eight instructions and you can verify the constant by hand. The new state is stored back at EBP-0x4C and doubles as the destination address.

The spread loop

push 10h                 ; tolen = sizeof(sockaddr_in)
lea  eax, [ebp-50h]      ; to
push eax
xor  ecx, ecx
push ecx                 ; flags = 0
xor  cx, 0178h           ; len = 376
push ecx
lea  eax, [ebp+3]        ; buf = start of worm body
push eax
mov  eax, [ebp-54h]      ; socket
push eax
call esi                 ; sendto(s, buf, 376, 0, &to, 16)
jmp  short PRNG          ; never returns

Single datagram, no handshake, no reply expected. That's why it spread so fast: with UDP there's nothing to wait on, so the only limit is how quickly sendto can be called and how fast the uplink is.

wg2 vs. Slammer

                wg2 (RAT)               Slammer-style worm
language        C++                     hand-written asm shellcode
size            full PE32               376 bytes
transport       HTTP/HTTPS (TCP)        one UDP datagram
control         C2 loop, 11 commands    none
persistence     beacon loop             none (memory only)
goal            remote administration   replicate

Detection and defense notes

  • Network: a host sending a flood of identical ~376-byte UDP packets to port 1434 across wide address ranges is the whole signature. Flow-based detection (fan-out rate to one port) works even if the payload changes.
  • Exposure: the resolution service shouldn't be reachable from untrusted networks. Filtering 1434/udp at the edge stops this outright.
  • Memory-only: nothing touches disk, so file-based AV has nothing to scan. Patching the SQL Server flaw is the real fix.
  • Analysis tip: when a sample has no imports and a wall of push imm32 ASCII, decode the stack strings first. The rest of the logic falls out of those names.

What I took away

  • Drawing the stack diagram first made the disassembly readable. Without it, every [ebp-xx] is a mystery.
  • Tiny does not mean simple. Null-byte avoidance shaped almost every instruction choice.
  • Comparing it with wg2 clarified how different "malware" can be: one waits for orders, the other never stops to listen.

item.title: Tearing Down wg2: An HTTP RAT in Ghidra
item.description:
For my reverse engineering course I took apart wg2, a 32-bit Windows RAT, function by function in Ghidra. This is the condensed version of my annotated decompilation: how it hides its C2, how it talks home, and the eleven commands it gives an attacker.

Ghidra's FUN_ names are kept so you can follow along in your own copy. The C2 domain is defanged.

First look

format     PE32, 4 sections (.text .rdata .data .rsrc)
language   C++ (connection object with a vtable)
network    WinINet, HTTP and HTTPS
built      2011-11-17 (and it tells you: see "version")

Call graph, in the order I walked it

entry()
 └─ FUN_0040297d  WinMain: decode C2, name the victim, beacon loop
     └─ FUN_00401406  command_and_control  (the heart)
         ├─ FUN_0040101c  build connection object
         ├─ FUN_004010c0  connect (InternetOpen/Connect/OpenRequest)
         ├─ FUN_004012c5  POST data + SSL bypass
         └─ switch → shell, list, kill, getf/putf, start, pidrun, geturl ...

Hiding the C2 with one bit

The C2 hostname sits in .data obfuscated: every byte was shifted left by one. Decoding is a right shift and a mask.

for (i = 0; i < len; i++)
    url[i] = (enc[i] >> 1) & 0x7F;
// -> stratos[.]mcafeepaying[.]com

That's not encryption, it's just enough to keep the domain out of strings. Note the domain itself pretending to be an antivirus vendor.

It then builds a URL path from the victim's hostname via GetComputerNameA (/VICTIM-PC/), so the C2 knows exactly which machine is calling. The main loop calls the C2 handler, then sleeps sleep_scalar × 60000 ms, until a global stop flag is set.

Talking home

FUN_0040101c builds a C++ connection object (about 0x28 bytes): three WinINet handles, a one-hour timeout, the URL path, hostname, a Mozilla/4.0 User-Agent, extra headers, and an HTTPS flag.

+0x00 vtable      +0x14 url path     +0x20 headers
+0x04 hInternet   +0x18 hostname     +0x24 https flag
+0x08 hConnect    +0x1C user-agent
+0x0C hRequest    +0x10 timeout (3,600,000 ms)

FUN_004010c0 is textbook WinINet: InternetOpenA → set send/connect/receive timeouts → InternetConnectA on port 80 or 443 → HttpOpenRequestA. The headers include Pragma: no-cache and a custom Computer: header with the hostname. That custom header is a great network IOC.

The SSL bypass

FUN_004012c5 POSTs data to the C2. If HttpSendRequestA fails with 12045 (ERROR_INTERNET_INVALID_CA), it doesn't give up:

if (GetLastError() == 12045) {               // 0x2F0D: bad cert
    InternetQueryOptionA(h, 31, &flags, &n);  // INTERNET_OPTION_SECURITY_FLAGS
    flags |= SECURITY_FLAG_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_CA;
    InternetSetOptionA(h, 31, &flags, 4);
    // ...and retry
}

So the operator can run HTTPS C2 on a self-signed certificate and still get encrypted traffic past anyone not doing TLS inspection.

The C2 loop

FUN_00401406 connects (five tries, 60 s apart), creates two anonymous pipes for a future shell, changes its working directory to C:\Windows\tasks to blend in, and announces itself with "<hostname> Connected!". Then it loops: POST pending output, read the reply, split it on spaces, and match the first token against a command table (8-byte entries starting at 0x0040402C).

case  command  what it does
0     shell    hidden cmd.exe, stdin/stdout/stderr over pipes
1     list     /p processes  /s services  /d drives
2     kill     /p PID        /s stop service
3     getf     fetch a file from the C2 and write it to disk
4     putf     read a local file, POST it to the C2 in 128 KB chunks
5     start    /p process (hidden window)  /s service
6     whoami   GetUserNameExA, DOMAIN\user
7     sleep    change the beacon interval
8     version  returns "20111117"
9     pidrun   run a command with another process's token
10    geturl   URLDownloadToFileA from any URL
-     other    piped to the shell, or "Start shell first."

Shell and token theft

FUN_00401BA9 finds cmd.exe via %ComSpec% (falling back to System32), sets STARTF_USESTDHANDLES | STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW with SW_HIDE, and wires the pipes in. If a PID is given, it escalates instead:

h = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, 0, pid);
OpenProcessToken(h, TOKEN_QUERY | TOKEN_DUPLICATE | TOKEN_ASSIGN_PRIMARY, &tok);
CreateProcessAsUserA(tok, NULL, "cmd.exe", ...);   // shell as that user

pidrun (FUN_004027A8 / FUN_00402817) reuses the same three calls to run any command under a stolen token. Point it at a SYSTEM process and a low-privilege foothold becomes SYSTEM.

Everything else

  • list: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot + Process32First/Next for processes (the same APIs I saw in anti-VM checks), EnumServicesStatusExA called twice (size, then data) for services, GetLogicalDrives + GetDriveTypeA + GetVolumeInformationA for drives.
  • kill / start: TerminateProcess, or the Service Control Manager with ControlService / StartServiceA, with friendly error messages for 0x420, 0x424 and 0x426.
  • getf / putf: runs in its own thread with its own connection and a different User-Agent (Mozilla/5.0), strips HTTP headers at the \r\n\r\n boundary.
  • geturl: a one-liner around URLDownloadToFileA, which lets the operator stage more tools from anywhere.

IOCs and detection ideas

network   stratos[.]mcafeepaying[.]com
          HTTP header "Computer: <hostname>"
          GET /<HOSTNAME>/ then POSTs, User-Agent Mozilla/4.0 and 5.0
host      process with cwd C:\Windows\tasks
          hidden cmd.exe whose parent isn't explorer.exe
          CreateProcessAsUser from a non-service process
strings   "Start shell first."  "Shell started successfully!"
          "Syntax error! Usage: GetUrl URL FileName"  "20111117"

What I took away

  • Twelve malicious behaviors, zero exploits. It's all documented Windows API, which is exactly why API-sequence detection beats signature matching.
  • Reading order matters. Starting from entry() and following the calls made a 600-line decompile readable in an afternoon.
  • Naming things in Ghidra as you go (initialize_array, send_get, create_shell) is most of the work. Once the struct offsets had names, the C2 loop basically read itself.

item.title: Building a Seven-VM Enterprise Homelab on Proxmox
item.description:
I wanted a place to practice attacking and defending something that looks like a real company network, so I built one at home on Proxmox. This post walks through the design and what I learned setting it up.

The lab

Seven VMs, split across isolated subnets:

  • pfSense as the firewall, handling rules, DHCP and NAT between segments
  • Kali Linux as the attacker box
  • Metasploitable 2 and DVWA / WebGoat (in Docker) as intentionally vulnerable targets
  • Windows Server 2022 as the Active Directory domain controller
  • A domain-joined Windows 11 workstation
  • Security Onion as the SIEM, watching traffic in real time

Remote access

Rather than opening ports, I used Tailscale with subnet routing so I can reach the lab from anywhere without exposing it to the internet.

tailscale up --advertise-routes=10.10.0.0/24,10.20.0.0/24

What's next

Future posts will cover attacking the AD domain from Kali and seeing what Security Onion actually catches.

Source and notes on GitHub →

item.title: Troubleshooting a Finance Share "Access Denied"
item.description:
A classic help-desk ticket, reproduced in my Enterprise IT Support Lab: a user can sign in to the domain and reach the Finance share, but gets "access denied" when opening it.

Working the ticket

  1. Reproduced the problem from the domain-joined workstation
  2. Checked the user's Active Directory group membership
  3. Found they were missing from Finance-Share-Read
  4. Added them to the group
  5. Had them sign out and back in so Windows issued a fresh security token
  6. Confirmed access to the share
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Finance-Share-Read" -Members "atest"
Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership atest | Select-Object Name

Why sign-out matters

Group membership is baked into the access token at logon. Adding someone to a group does nothing for their current session, which is one of the most common reasons a "fixed" permission still looks broken.

The share used both share-level and NTFS permissions, which is a good reminder that Windows access control is layered: the most restrictive one wins.

item.title: Patching Out Anti-VM Checks in Malware Samples
item.description:
Some malware refuses to run when it detects a virtual machine, which is a problem when a VM is exactly where you want to analyze it. In my malware analysis labs I ran into samples using the old SIDT, SLDT and STR tricks.

How the checks work

These instructions return the locations of CPU descriptor tables. On older hypervisors those locations differ from bare metal in predictable ways, so the sample compares the result against a known value and bails out if it looks virtual.

Patching

Using IDA Pro and Ghidra, I found the comparison after each check and patched the conditional jump so the sample always takes the "real hardware" path.

; before
sidt  [esp+idtr]
cmp   byte ptr [esp+idtr+5], 0FFh
je    looks_like_vm
; after: je -> nop nop

Other things I looked at

  • PE structure and packing
  • Anti-debug techniques
  • Polymorphic vs. metamorphic behavior in a RAT and a SQL worm

item.title: Reconstructing a Data Exfiltration: The HiTek Forensics Challenge
item.description:
The HiTek Forensics Challenge was the capstone exercise in my Digital Forensics course at LSU. My team of five got two disk images, a Windows workstation and an Ubuntu server, plus one packet capture, and a single question: what left the building, how, and who did it?

Forensics is a reconstruction problem. You work backwards from artifacts to events, the artifacts are incomplete (sometimes on purpose), and every conclusion has to point at a specific piece of evidence. This is how we rebuilt the case.

The scene

host          ip            os           role
WIN-WS-01     192.168.0.6   Windows      suspect's workstation
web-srv-02    192.168.0.8   Ubuntu       FTP + web server (staging)
(unnamed)     192.168.0.4   Mac OS X     retrieval machine

Toolkit: FTK Imager and Autopsy for the disks, Wireshark for network.pcapng, John the Ripper, impacket-secretsdump and CrackStation for credentials, and plain Linux tools for the logs.

Step 1: get everyone's passwords

Recovering credentials early meant we could tie each action in the logs and the capture to a specific account instead of guessing.

  • Ubuntu: pulled the SHA-512 hashes from /etc/shadow and ran John with rockyou.
  • Windows: exported the SAM and SYSTEM hives with Autopsy, dumped NT hashes with secretsdump, and fed them to CrackStation.
$ john --wordlist=rockyou.txt shadow.txt
$ impacket-secretsdump -sam SAM -system SYSTEM LOCAL

account      box        password
webmaster    ubuntu     password
cknight      ubuntu     popcorn
carson       windows    123456     (admin)
jonathan     windows    letmein
tester       windows    monkey     (hint: "the zoo")

Every password was in the top of any wordlist. That's a finding on its own, separate from the case. The tester password was double-confirmed by its hint and a monkey picture sitting in the browser cache, which is the kind of detail that makes forensics fun.

Step 2: the night before (Nov 27)

auth.log and the webmaster's bash history showed a login at 23:13. Over the next 24 minutes:

sudo apt-get install apache2 apache2-doc apache2-utils
sudo apt-get install vsftpd
sudo nano /etc/vsftpd.conf
sudo apt-get install mysql-server
echo "create database website;" | mysql -u root -p
sudo chmod 777 /var/www      # <- the important one
ifconfig

chmod 777 on the web root means anything dropped in over FTP is instantly downloadable over HTTP by anyone, no login needed. The server was being set up as an open staging point the night before anything was stolen.

Step 3: the exfil (Nov 28)

File metadata on the Windows image showed two password-protected archives, secrets.zip and BusinessStrategy.zip, created around 15:45. The capture picks it up from there. FTP is plaintext, so Wireshark showed the login, the credentials and the file names outright.

ftp || ftp-data
ip.addr == 192.168.0.6 && ip.addr == 192.168.0.8
ip.src == 192.168.0.4 && http
Nov 27 23:13  webmaster logs in to web-srv-02, installs apache2/vsftpd/mysql
Nov 27 23:37  chmod 777 /var/www
Nov 28 ~15:45 secrets.zip + BusinessStrategy.zip created on WIN-WS-01
Nov 28 15:46:30  STOR BusinessStrategy.zip  .6 -> .8 (as webmaster)
Nov 28 15:52:06  STOR secrets.zip           .6 -> .8 (as webmaster)
Nov 28 >15:52    HTTP GET both zips         .4 -> .8 (no auth)
Nov 28 after     zips deleted from WIN-WS-01 and /var/www
Nov 28 17:52:02  web-srv-02 shuts down

Three hops: compress on Windows, stage on the Ubuntu box over FTP, pull from the web server with a Mac.

Step 4: the cover-up that didn't work

  • Deletion: both ZIPs were deleted from the workstation and the server. On NTFS, deleting a file only marks its clusters free. Nothing had overwritten them yet, so Autopsy carved both archives back out of unallocated space.
  • Encryption: the archives were password-protected, so we could prove what moved by name and metadata but not what was inside.
  • Ambiguity: chmod 777 looks like a lazy admin mistake. Without the rest of the timeline it would have been easy to wave off.

Step 5: who

Several independent threads point at carson:

  • The FTP uploads came from 192.168.0.6, carson's workstation.
  • They used the same webmaster credentials that configured the server the night before, and carson, as a Windows admin, had the access to get them.
  • Evaluations.odt in carson's Documents held a supervisor note about carson installing the wrong VMware version on every office machine: a history of misusing admin access and a plausible grudge. Projects.odt confirmed the IT role.
  • The other accounts came up clean. tester was just browsing (YouTube, Google, Amazon, starwars.com) and jonathan had nothing in the window. Ruling people out mattered as much as ruling carson in.

What the evidence doesn't prove

I think being honest about the gaps is part of the job. We proved the activity came from carson's machine with webmaster credentials, not that carson was physically at the keyboard. A real case would need physical access logs, interviews, and a check for remote access. And without the ZIP passwords, we never confirmed what data was actually inside the archives.

Takeaways

  • No malware, no exploit. Everything here was apt, FTP, a web server and a delete key. An insider with admin rights can do this on most networks.
  • Signatures would have missed it. No bad hashes, no bad IPs. What was detectable was behavior: an admin creating archives and immediately moving them out, then deleting them. That's a UEBA / DLP problem, not an antivirus one.
  • Deletion isn't destruction. Without overwriting the sectors, deleted files are just waiting to be carved.
  • The story is the deliverable. Each artifact alone is ambiguous. Lined up in order and tied to accounts and timestamps, they tell one story.

We delivered a full investigative report with a relationship map of every user, host and transfer, plus a presentation. Rebuilding it here was a good excuse to re-read the bash history one more time.

I'm a Computer Science student at LSU concentrating in cybersecurity. Most of what I learn happens in labs, CTF-style challenges and my homelab, and most of it disappears into notes nobody reads, including me.

item.title: Room'r: Roommate Matching with Flutter and Firebase
item.description:
Room'r is a team-built, swipe-style roommate matching app for incoming college students. You answer a lifestyle questionnaire, set a couple of dealbreakers, swipe on profiles, and chat with the people who like you back. It's written in Flutter with Firebase behind it, targeting web, desktop and Android from one codebase.

The flow

sign up -> profile -> photo -> questionnaire -> dealbreakers
  -> swipe deck -> mutual like = match -> chat -> push notification

Stack

  • Flutter with Riverpod for state and go_router for navigation, running on Chrome, Windows and Android.
  • Firebase: Auth for accounts, Firestore for profiles, matches and messages, Storage for photos, Messaging for push.
  • Cloud Functions that fire when a match or a message is created, look up both users, send the notification and prune dead device tokens.

How matching works

Compatibility is a transparent weighted score from 0 to 100, not a black box:

sleep schedule   20%     study habits   15%     substances     10%
cleanliness      20%     noise          15%     guests         10%
pets + temperature 10%

Each category compares two answers. Scales (cleanliness, noise) lose points by how far apart they are. Categories like sleep schedule are more forgiving: early bird against night owl scores 20, but a "flexible" answer scores 70 with anyone. The total maps to a label from "Low Match" to "Perfect Match".

Dealbreakers

Each user can pick up to two (no smoking, no pets, no night owls, and so on). The swipe deck filters on them in both directions: if either person's dealbreaker is triggered by the other, neither sees the other. That's the kind of rule that sounds easy and then turns out to need careful thought.

Icebreakers

The chat suggests conversation starters built from the pair's two profiles, so shared interests give you a better question. Each branch has several variations, plus a large pool of general ones, and the service cycles through unseen questions before repeating any.

Things I learned

  • Putting the scoring in one small, pure service made it easy to reason about and to test.
  • Server-side triggers are the right place for notifications. The client can't reliably know about a match that another user created.
  • Config files for Firebase are generated per developer and never committed, which is the right call. It just means the setup guide matters as much as the code.

It was a team build with a prototype, a setup guide and a full app. The source repo belongs to a teammate, so I haven't linked it here.

item.title: Designing a Supermarket Database (and Its Checkout Transaction)
item.description:
For my database systems course, my team designed and built a multi-branch supermarket database and a command-line checkout app on top of it. The point was to practice the whole pipeline: requirements, an E-R diagram, a relational schema, test data, SQL queries and an application that actually uses them.

The problem

A supermarket chain with several branches needs one place to keep prices, stock and sales. Without it, every branch tracks everything by hand, and nobody can see revenue or stock across the company.

Relational schema

StoreBranch(branch_id PK, name, address, phone)
Product(product_id PK, name, barcode UNIQUE, unit_price, is_active, category)
Inventory(branch_id PK/FK, product_id PK/FK, quantity)
Sale(sale_id PK, branch_id FK, sale_datetime, total_amount)
SaleItem(sale_id PK/FK, product_id PK/FK, quantity, unit_price, discount)
  • Inventory is a junction table with a composite key, so the same product can be stocked at many branches with a different quantity at each.
  • SaleItem copies unit_price at the time of sale. That way, changing a price later never rewrites history.
  • Foreign keys are switched on (PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON), because SQLite doesn't enforce them by default.

The checkout transaction

The part I find most interesting is checkout. It has to either completely happen or not happen at all, so it runs inside one transaction: check stock for every item in the cart again, insert the sale, insert each sale line, and subtract inventory. If anything fails, the whole thing rolls back.

BEGIN;
  -- re-check stock for every cart item
  INSERT INTO Sale (branch_id, sale_datetime, total_amount) VALUES (?, datetime('now'), ?);
  INSERT INTO SaleItem (...) VALUES (...);          -- per cart line
  UPDATE Inventory SET quantity = quantity - ? WHERE branch_id = ? AND product_id = ?;
COMMIT;   -- any error: ROLLBACK

Re-checking stock inside the transaction matters: the stock you saw when you added to the cart may not be what's left when you pay.

Reports

Queries live in a plain queries.sql file, each tagged with -- name: .... The app loads them by name and runs them from a Statistics menu, so adding a report means adding SQL and not changing Python.

-- revenue by category
SELECT p.category,
       ROUND(SUM((si.unit_price - si.discount) * si.quantity), 2) AS revenue
FROM SaleItem si
JOIN Product p ON si.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;

There are 16 in total, including sales history, revenue per day, top sellers, low stock, inventory value per product, and products that never sold (a LEFT JOIN with WHERE ... IS NULL).

The app

=== LSU Market CLI ===
1. List available products
2. Add product to cart
3. View cart
4. Checkout
5. Statistics
6. Exit

Python with SQLite, a plain menu, and a seeded sample dataset of products, stock and sales. The repo includes the schema, data, queries and a rebuild guide so anyone can recreate the database from scratch in four commands.

What I'd improve

  • Use parameterized queries everywhere (checkout already does) and move the statistics menu to a loop instead of one block per report.
  • Add indexes on the sale date and on SaleItem.product_id once the data grows.
  • Track stock changes in their own table (receiving, returns, shrinkage) so inventory is auditable and not just a number that goes down.

It was a team project, and my part was the data generation, the relational schema and the written report. Source: CSC4402-Supermarket.

item.title: ERU: Building a Social Feed with Spring Boot, MongoDB and React Native
item.description:
ERU was a team project for a software course in fall 2024: a social media app built to put curated, worthwhile posts where doomscrolling usually is. We built a Java backend, a TypeScript frontend and a MongoDB database, and got a working feed, uploads, comments and profiles by the deadline.

Architecture

React Native (Expo, web)  --HTTP/JSON-->  Spring Boot REST API  -->  MongoDB
  feed, upload, explore,                    accounts, posts,
  profile, settings, FAQ                    comments, likes
  • Frontend: TypeScript and React Native via Expo, run in the browser. Components for posts, comments, likes and a nav bar, with pages for the home feed, upload, explore, profile and settings.
  • Backend: Java 21 with Spring Boot, controllers per area (accounts, friends, and so on) and a centralized exception handler that returns consistent error models.
  • Data: MongoDB, wrapped in a single manager class so the rest of the code never touches the driver directly.

The API

GET   /account/{id}            profile
GET   /account/{id}/feed       one user's posts, newest first
GET   /account/feed            home feed, newest first
POST  /account/post            create a post (UUID assigned server-side)
POST  /post/{id}/like          like
POST  /post/{id}/comment       comment

New post IDs are random UUIDs, and the server re-rolls on the (astronomically unlikely) collision. The feed endpoint also fills in each post's author name and picture so the client doesn't need a second call.

On the frontend

The home feed loads posts, tracks which identifiers it has already seen so repeated fetches never duplicate a post, and falls back to defaults for missing captions or profile pictures instead of crashing on incomplete data.

What was unfinished (and honest about it)

  • No login or registration screen. We hardcoded one account ID, so profile pages show that user.
  • The Explore tab shows placeholder images; the recommendation algorithm never got built.
  • The front end talks to localhost addresses, so it's a dev setup and not a deployable one.

Lessons

  • Cutting scope early beats cutting features at the deadline. The unfinished list above is what scope creep looks like.
  • Never commit secrets. The repo's config file shipped with a database connection string. Credentials belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, and anything that has been committed has to be rotated, even if the repo is deleted later.
  • Typed models on both ends (Java classes, TypeScript interfaces) caught a lot of mismatches before runtime.

Source: CSC-3380 Team-4.

item.title: JavaShooter: My First Game, and What I'd Fix Now
item.description:
JavaShooter was my first real project: an infinite roguelike shooter written in Java for a course in spring 2024. There's no ending. You clear a level, earn a level-up point, spend it, and try to see how far you can get. It's also where I learned that "it works" and "it's well built" are two different milestones.

How it plays

move     W A S D
shoot    left click (or space)
enemies  regular  - drift around the board
         chaser   - a red diamond that homes in on you
         boss     - 5 hit points, shoots back every 2 seconds
upgrade  after each level: player speed | bullet speed | shield

Every level adds two more regular enemies, another chaser and another boss. There's no cap, so the game gets harder until you lose. After each clear you pick one upgrade, so you're always choosing between running faster, shooting faster, or taking an extra hit.

What's under the hood

  • Sprite engine: built on the sprite and collision library from the course, so I wrote game rules and not a renderer.
  • Collision listeners: one listener per pair (enemy and bullet, boss and bullet, enemy bullet and player, and so on) decides who dies and what happens next.
  • Chaser AI: every 2 seconds the chaser takes the vector to the player, normalizes it, and heads that way at a fixed speed. That's about ten lines of vector math.
  • Progression: a NewLevels class clears the board and respawns everything with higher counts.
  • Feedback: sound effects on shots and kills, a brief invincibility window after you clear a level, and a retry prompt when you lose.
// the chaser, in spirit
dx = player.x - x;  dy = player.y - y;
d  = sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy);
setVel(dx / d * SPEED, dy / d * SPEED);

What I'd do differently now

Looking back with a bit more experience, these are the lessons I'd hand my past self:

  • Share the win/lose code. The "you lose, retry?" logic is copied across four collision listeners, and the level-clear logic is copied twice. One method would've been easier to fix and extend.
  • Don't use blocking dialogs in a game loop. Popups for win, lose and upgrade pause everything and break the flow. An in-game overlay would feel much better.
  • Don't use static state for player stats. Things like shield strength being static made restart bugs easy to introduce. They belong on the player object.
  • Use one game clock. Each enemy and boss starts its own timer thread. A single update loop would be easier to reason about and to pause.
  • Keep build output out of the repo. The repo is a zipped IDE project with compiled classes in it. A .gitignore and plain source files would be much friendlier to read.

Why it still matters to me

It was the first time I built something other people could actually play, and it taught me game loops, collision handling, simple AI and how quickly "just one more feature" turns into spaghetti. Those lessons are the reason I want to build a second one: JavaShooter 2 is on my roadmap.

Source: github.com/nrodrigue2004/JavaShooter
